focus: Shannon (1949), Communication in the Presence of Noise, Section II, Theorem 1. Explain sampling and aliasing using a single sinusoid. Show the continuous signal, the samples, the Nyquist frequency and the apparent frequency of the sampled signal. Let the learner change the signal frequency and the sampling rate. Guide them through sampling above twice the signal frequency and sampling below it. Check that the apparent frequency equals the true frequency below the Nyquist frequency and that a signal at exactly the sampling rate appears as zero frequency; handle a sampling rate equal to twice the signal frequency.
audience: Second-year engineering undergraduates who know sine waves.
excerpt: (paraphrased) Theorem 1: If a function f(t) contains no frequencies higher than W cycles per second, it is completely determined by giving its ordinates at a series of points spaced 1/(2W) seconds apart. A rate of 2W samples per second therefore suffices; half the sampling rate is commonly called the Nyquist frequency. A component at a frequency above half the sampling rate cannot be distinguished from samples alone: a sinusoid at frequency f sampled at rate fs gives the same samples as one at |f - k fs| for an integer k, and reconstruction yields the lowest such frequency, which is called an alias.
